Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath
Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
Medical equipment such as needles or drips

Maladaptive Strategies.value: control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'Reminders of victims' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type; it implies exposure to other victims in a disaster/assault context rather than illness-related trauma.

'Being naked' as a trigger is difficult to connect to life-threatening illness unless there is a very specific medical context; with the other selected items it appears context-incongruent rather than illness-linked.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding appraisal or threat items about humiliation, criticism, or social danger; this strategy is poorly matched to the rest of the profile.

'Being naked' is a poor fit as a primary trigger for a life-threatening illness profile unless the illness/trauma specifically involved exposure or bodily vulnerability in that context; with the rest of this profile centered on somatic and medical cues, this item stands out as clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Rehearsing conversations before any interaction suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety or interpersonal threat management, which is not supported by the other selected trigger, memory, appraisal, or threat items and does not fit the stated illness-centered formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
issues.explanation: Always choosing a safe/protected seat implies environmental danger monitoring more typical of assault/combat/public threat trauma than life-threatening illness; it is weakly connected to the medical/somatic trigger pattern here.

issues.item: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
issues.explanation: For a 37-year-old man with trauma centered on a life-threatening illness, the threat profile is otherwise strongly somatic/medical (negative emotions, body on alert) and the trigger/strategy pattern is specifically tied to breathlessness, procedures, and medical cues. A prominent exaggerated startle to ordinary sounds is not impossible, but in this profile it appears disconnected from the illness-related trigger network and from the cognitive formulation, where Threat is mainly linked with Maladaptive Strategies rather than a broad sensory hypervigilance pattern. This makes the item clinically incoherent relative to the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Mark, a 37-year-old database administrator, presented as a man holding himself perfectly still, as if a sudden movement might shatter him. It had been eighteen months since he was discharged from the ICU after a near-fatal bout of acute respiratory distress syndrome, an experience that had left his body healed but his mind besieged. He had survived, but he had come to believe his own body was the most dangerous place he could be. The memories were not of the illness itself, but of the fight for control in a sterile, beeping room: the suffocating pressure in his chest, the ventilator tube forcing air into his lungs, and the constant, dispassionate presence of needles and IV drips tethering him to life. He remembered the sheer terror of being unable to draw a full breath, a sensation of drowning on dry land that had become the central organizing principle of his fear.

After returning home, Mark found that the hospital had followed him. He lived in a state of hypervigilant alert, his body perpetually tense, braced for the next internal betrayal. He was terrified of strong negative feelings, convinced that a surge of fear or anger could trigger a relapse, a physical collapse from which he wouldn't recover. This profound sense of threat dictated his every move, leading him to construct a life of rigid, protective avoidance. He stopped exercising immediately, fearing the pounding of his heart and the quickening of his breath. He cancelled all his follow-up medical appointments, unable to bear the sight of a clinic or the touch of a stethoscope. The only way he felt he could exert any influence over his treacherous physiology was by controlling what went into it; his diet became a spartan, meticulously managed ritual, a small island of order in a sea of bodily chaos.

These strategies, designed for self-preservation, have paradoxically tightened the net of his anxiety. His avoidance of all physical activity has led to significant deconditioning. Now, simply climbing the single flight of stairs to his apartment leaves him winded, his lungs burning. This somatic sensation of breathlessness, a direct result of his inactivity, has become his most potent trigger, plunging him back into the panic of the ICU. In these moments, his heart hammers against his ribs, sweat slicks his skin, and he is certain he is dying all over again.

Furthermore, his refusal to engage with any medical care has amplified his sense of ambient threat. Every minor ache, cough, or dizzy spell, which he might once have ignored, now registers as a potential catastrophe. Without a doctor to offer reassurance or a diagnosis, his mind runs wild with worst-case scenarios, leaving him in a constant state of unverified dread. This chronic worry keeps his body on high alert, creating a self-sustaining feedback loop where the strategies he uses to manage his fear only serve to make the world-and his own body-feel more dangerous. This withdrawal from life ultimately cost him his marriage; his ex-wife, he explained quietly, grew tired of living with a ghost.

He finally sought therapy after an incident at work. Rushing to a meeting, he took the stairs and was overcome by such intense breathlessness and chest pain that he collapsed, convinced he was having a heart attack. It was a panic attack, but the experience shattered his illusion of control. He now understands that his fortress of avoidance has become a prison, and he is desperate to escape. Yet, he is terrified that the path to recovery involves deliberately walking toward the very physical sensations he believes will kill him.
